title: Matching a Rule to Whole Lines
short: A rule of inference applies only to whole lines whose main connectives match the rule's pattern, with any formulas in place of p, q, r and s.
trouble: Learners apply MP inside a line: from (p → q) ∨ r and p they infer q. Rules of inference never work on a part of a line.

blocks.html: Each rule of inference is a pattern written with $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$. In a real proof, those letters stand for whatever formulas fill their places. This lesson makes the matching exact, using the rules from Constructive Dilemma (CD).

A rule of inference applies to whole lines whose main connectives fit the rule's pattern, with any formulas in place of $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$ (the same formula wherever the same letter appears). It never applies to a part of a line.

Validity depends only on form, so if MP is valid for letters, it is valid for any formulas put in place of those letters: the truth table for the bigger argument has the same pattern of T and F in the columns that matter. But a part of a line is not asserted on its own. In $(p \to q) \lor r$, the conditional $p \to q$ might be false (when $r$ is true), so using it as if it were a premise could take you from truths to a falsehood.

blocks.title: Match the main connectives
blocks.q: Which rule takes $(p \land q) \to \neg r$ and $p \land q$ to $\neg r$?
steps: Line 1's main connective is $\to$; line 2 is exactly its antecedent.
MP's $p$ is $p \land q$ and its $q$ is $\neg r$.

blocks.title: A part of a line
blocks.q: Can MP take $(p \to q) \lor r$ and $p$ to $q$?
steps: The conditional is only a part.
blocks.a: No. No rule of inference applies to line 1 as it stands.

blocks.title: Same letter, same formula
blocks.q: Does HS take $p \to q$ and $r \to s$ to $p \to s$?
steps: HS needs the consequent of the first to be the antecedent of the second.

blocks.html: Applying MP inside a line: from $(p \to q) \lor r$ and $p$, inferring $q$. Check the main connective of each cited line before you name a rule. If the line is a disjunction, MP, MT and HS cannot use it; if it is a conditional, Simp cannot.

A useful habit is to draw an imaginary box around each big part. In $(p \lor q) \to (r \land \neg s)$ the antecedent $p \lor q$ is one box and the consequent $r \land \neg s$ another; the line is then just box $\to$ box, and MP or MT can see it plainly. The rules never look inside a box; they only check how the boxes are joined.

head: Rule
Main connective of the cited lines
rows: one conditional (and its antecedent, or the negation of its consequent)
one conjunction of conditionals and one disjunction
